fetched_contents.text: Antioxidant Activity of Anthocyanins and Anthocyanidins: A Critical Review Abstract Anthocyanins are the main plant pigments responsible for the color of flowers, fruits, and vegetative organs of many plants, and are applied also as safe food colorants. They are efficient antioxidants. In this review, the reactivity of anthocyanins and their aglycones, anthocyanidins, in the main antioxidant assays, and their reactions with reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, effects of interactions with other compounds and metal ions on the antioxidant activity of anthocyanins and the electrochemical properties of anthocyanins are presented. Numerous cases of attenuation of oxidative stress at the cellular and organismal levels by anthocyanins are cited. The direct and indirect antioxidant action of anthocyanins, the question of the specificity of anthocyanin action in complex extracts, as well as limitations of cellular in vitro assays and biomarkers used for the detection of antioxidant effects of anthocyanins, are critically discussed. Keywords: antioxidant, antioxidant assays, indirect antioxidant effect, oxidative stress, reactive oxygen species, biomarkers 1. Introduction Anthocyanins (from the Greek anthos, flower and kianos, blue), a class of flavonoids, are the most important pigments of vascular plants. They are responsible for the shiny orange, pink, red, violet, and blue colors of flowers and fruits, but also of vegetative organs of many plants. Anthocyanins have many diverse functions within plants. Synthesis of anthocyanins in petals is intended to attract pollinators, whereas anthocyanins in seeds and fruits may aid in seed dispersal. Anthocyanins and other flavonoids can also be important as feeding deterrents and in the protection against damage from UV irradiation and other stresses [1,2,3,4]. Anthocyanins and their derivatives are the crucial pigments responsible for the red wine color [5,6]. As all flavonoids, they are efficient antioxidants and exert many beneficial health effects, which may depend on or be independent of, their antioxidant action [7,8,9]. They are used as safe food colorants, with no adverse effects on consumers, in contrast to many synthetic pigments [10,11]. The best nutritional sources of anthocyanins are berries such as strawberries, blueberries, blackberries, blackcurrants, redcurrants, and raspberries. The highest anthocyanin content is found in elderberries and chokeberries. Other good sources of anthocyanins include purple corn, cherries, plums, pomegranates, eggplants, wine, grapes, and red/purple vegetables such as black carrots, red cabbage, purple cauliflower, maqui, myrtle, and açai [12,13,14,15,16]. Anthocyanins present in plants are O-glycosides of aglycons (anthocyanidins) and sugars. Anthocyanidins differ in substituents on the flavylium (2-phenylbenzopyrylium) skeleton. From among 31 identified anthocyanidins present in about 700 anthocyanins, six are the most common (Figure 1). Anthocyanins have a sugar residue linked to an anthocyanidin in position C3 of the aglycone, via an α- or β-glycosidic bond. If additional sugar residues are present in the anthocyanin molecule, they are linked in positions C5 and C7, and less frequently in positions C3′ and C5′. The sugar residues are usually glucose, galactose, rhamnose, arabinose, or xylose. Anthocyanin molecules can be additionally acylated with cinnamic acids (especially cinnamic or caffeic acid, but also ferulic or sinapic acid), acetic, malic, malonic, oxalic, or succinic acid [17,18,19]. Glycosylation increases the stability and water solubility of anthocyanidins. Increasing the number of sugar residues seems to further increase the stability of the anthocyanin, which is explained by the higher stability of the network of intramolecular H-bonds within the sugar moiety, and between the sugar and the aglycone [20,21]. Anthocyanin glucosyl acylation by aliphatic and aromatic acids further increases their stability [22]. Similar to other flavonoids, anthocyanins and anthocyanidins are good antioxidants, due to the scavenging of free radicals and other reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS and RNS, respectively). This review summarizes the antioxidant activity of anthocyanins in cell-free systems, exemplifies their antioxidant effects on cells in vitro, in animal experiments, and in human studies (Figure 2), and discusses fields of uncertainty associated with these studies. 2. Anthocyanidins and Anthocyanins in the Popular Assays of Antioxidant Activity In general, the antioxidant activity of anthocyanins (as well as other antioxidants) is due to two mechanisms: hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) and single-electron transfer (SET). In the HAT mechanism, a free radical R• removes a hydrogen atom from the antioxidant. In this reaction, the free radical is converted into a more stable product and a free radical of the antioxidant A• is formed. In the SET mechanism, the antioxidant donates an electron to the free radical, also forming A•. These two mechanisms often operate simultaneously, and their contribution is determined by the antioxidant structure, solubility, the partition coefficients of the reactants, and the solvent polarity [23]. From among the most popular assays of antioxidant activity, the Oxygen Radical Absorbing Capacity (ORAC) assay [24,25] is a HAT-based assay of antioxidant activity, while the Ferric Reducing Antioxidant Power (FRAP) assay [26] and CUPric ion Reducing Antioxidant C apacity (CUPRAC) [27] are SET-based assays. 2,2 DiPhenyl-1-PicrylHydrazyl radical (DPPH•) decolorization [28] and 2,2′-Azinobis(3-ethyl-2,3-dihydroBenzoThiazole-6-sulphonate) radical (ABTS•) decolorization assays [29] may involve both SET and HAT reactions [30]. Authors Affiliation * 1 Antioxidants and DNA Damage Group, Rowett Research Institute, Aberdeen, Scotland, UK. * PMID: 11677035 * DOI: 10.1016/s0891-5849(01)00618-9 Abstract Anthocyanins are secondary plant metabolites responsible for the blue, purple, and red color of many plant tissues. The phenolic structure of anthocyanins conveys marked antioxidant activity in model systems via donation of electrons or hydrogen atoms from hydroxyl moieties to free radicals. Dietary intakes of anthocyanins may exceed 200 mg/day, however, little is known about their antioxidant potency in vivo. Consequently, the aim of this study was to establish whether anthocyanins could act as putative antioxidant micronutrients. Rats were maintained on vitamin E-deficient diets for 12 weeks in order to enhance susceptibility to oxidative damage and then repleted with rations containing a highly purified anthocyanin-rich extract at a concentration of 1 g/kg diet. The extract consisted of the 3-glucopyranoside forms of delphinidin, cyanidin, petunidin, peonidin, and malvidin. Consumption of the anthocyanin-repleted diet significantly improved (p <.01) plasma antioxidant capacity and decreased (p <.001) the vitamin E deficiency-enhanced hydroperoxides and 8-Oxo-deoxyguanosine concentrations in liver. These compounds are indices of lipid peroxidation and DNA damage, respectively. Dietary consumption of anthocyanin-rich foods may contribute to overall antioxidant status, particularly in areas of habitually low vitamin E intake. Abstract Phase II metabolic enzymes are a battery of critical proteins that detoxify xenobiotics by increasing their hydrophilicity and enhancing their disposal. These enzymes have long been studied for their preventative and protective effects against mutagens and carcinogens and for their regulation via the Keap1 (Kelch-like ECH associated protein 1) / Nrf2 (Nuclear factor erythroid 2 related factor 2) / ARE (antioxidant response elements) pathway. Recently, a series of studies have reported the altered expression of phase II genes in postmortem tissue of patients with various neurological diseases. These observations hint at a role for phase II enzymes in the evolution of such conditions. Anthocyanins exert antioxidant effects primarily through direct scavenging of free radicals and reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, with mechanisms explained by hydrogen atom transfer and single-electron transfer. The evidence states that anthocyanins and anthocyanidins are good antioxidants because they scavenge free radicals and other reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS and RNS), and that the antioxidant activity is due to two main mechanisms: hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) and single-electron transfer (SET) [N1-F1]. In HAT, a free radical removes a hydrogen atom from the antioxidant, converting the radical into a more stable product while forming a free radical of the antioxidant; in SET, the antioxidant donates an electron to the free radical, forming a radical of the antioxidant [N1-F1]. This dual mechanism explains how anthocyanins stabilize radicals by either donating hydrogen atoms or electrons [N1-R2].

The evidence also indicates that anthocyanins directly neutralize reactive species through direct antioxidant properties and indirectly via induction of intracellular Nrf2 pathways [N1-R3]. The direct scavenging is supported by the review’s discussion of anthocyanin reactivity with reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and their effects in antioxidant assays [N1-F1]. A separate search result notes that anthocyanins show peroxynitrite-scavenging activity, and the review also discusses nitroxides as stable free radicals with antioxidant properties, reinforcing the idea that anthocyanins can stabilize reactive species through radical stabilization rather than simply eliminating them [N1-R5].

Structure-activity relationships are evident in the evidence. The review notes that methylation of the 4′-OH group markedly reduced antioxidant activity, indicating that hydroxyl substituents on the anthocyanin skeleton are important for activity [N1-R4]. This supports the idea that anthocyanin structure determines reactivity: the presence and position of hydroxyl groups, glycosylation, and acylation all influence stability and antioxidant capacity [N1-F1]. The evidence also emphasizes that glycosylation increases stability and water solubility, and that increasing the number of sugar residues further increases stability by strengthening intramolecular hydrogen bonding and sugar-aglycone interactions [N1-F1]. These structural features likely underpin the ability of anthocyanins to donate hydrogen or electrons effectively in radical scavenging.

Overall, anthocyanins directly neutralize free radicals and reactive oxygen and nitrogen species through HAT and SET, donate hydrogen or electrons to stabilize radicals, and their antioxidant activity is strongly structure-dependent [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R4].

Anthocyanins enhance antioxidant enzyme activity primarily by upregulating phase II antioxidant enzymes and indirectly modulating transcription factors such as Nrf2. The evidence states that anthocyanins induce the activation of phase II enzymes through the Keap1/Nrf2/ARE pathway [N2-R3]. This pathway is central to antioxidant defense because Nrf2 regulates the expression of a multitude of antioxidant and phase II enzyme genes and is negatively regulated by Keap1 [N4-R4]. The review on Nrf2 and phase II enzymes explains that the activated Nrf2/ARE pathway boosts the expression of phase II genes either by Keap1-dependent or Keap1-independent means [N4-R1]. This provides a direct mechanism for how anthocyanins influence enzyme activity: by activating Nrf2 and thereby inducing phase II genes.

The enzymes upregulated or activated by anthocyanins include the phase II enzymes discussed in the Nrf2 review, such as glutathione S-transferase (GST), NAD(P)H: quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and other phase II enzymes involved in detoxification and elimination of oxidative stress [N4-F2]. The evidence also notes that Nrf2-regulated phase II enzymes have long been studied for their preventative and protective effects against mutagens and carcinogens [N4-R3]. In addition, the anthocyanin study specifically points to activation of phase II antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes, indicating that anthocyanins are not only direct scavengers but also enzyme inducers [N2-R3].

Anthocyanins influence transcription factors and signaling pathways through Nrf2-mediated regulation. The evidence clearly ties anthocyanin effects to the Keap1/Nrf2/ARE pathway, with Keap1 sequestering Nrf2 in the cytoplasm and preventing its downstream effects on phase II genes [N4-F2]. When Nrf2 is activated, it translocates to the nucleus and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE), thereby inducing the transcription of phase II genes [N4-F2]. This pathway context explains how anthocyanins can influence enzyme activity at the transcriptional level [N4-R1][N4-F2].

Dose- and context-dependent effects are also evident in the evidence. The anthocyanin study notes that anthocyanins can ameliorate human retinal capillary endothelial function by decreasing ROS and increasing the enzyme activity of catalase (CAT) [N2-R4]. This suggests that enzyme activation is not universal but depends on the tissue and condition. The review also highlights that anthocyanin effects are context-dependent because the contribution of HAT and SET mechanisms depends on structure, solubility, partition coefficients, and solvent polarity [N1-F1]. The broader review further states that anthocyanins may exert beneficial health effects that depend on or are independent of their antioxidant action [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence supports a dose- and context-dependent enhancement of antioxidant enzyme activity, with Nrf2-mediated induction of phase II enzymes as a central mechanism [N2-R3][N4-F2].

The evidence also shows effects on membrane integrity and oxidative damage markers. The anthocyanin-rich extract study reports a significant decrease in vitamin E deficiency-enhanced hydroperoxides and 8-oxo-deoxyguanosine concentrations in liver, indicating reduced oxidative stress markers and better protection against lipid peroxidation and DNA damage [N3-F3]. The review on oxidative stress and skin diseases notes that lipid peroxidation can provoke damage to biological macromolecules such as DNA, lipids, and proteins [N3-R2]. This implies that anthocyanins may improve membrane integrity by reducing the formation of peroxidation products that compromise membrane structure and function.

The evidence also distinguishes prevention versus repair of peroxidation damage. The anthocyanin-rich extract study shows that dietary anthocyanins improved plasma antioxidant capacity and decreased indices of lipid peroxidation, suggesting a preventive effect rather than a reparative one [N3-F3]. Instead, the strongest supported conclusion is that anthocyanins reduce peroxidation damage by lowering lipid peroxidation products such as MDA, reducing oxidative damage markers, and improving antioxidant status [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F3].

Overall, anthocyanins reduce lipid peroxidation products like MDA, lower oxidative damage markers, and appear to act primarily as preventers of peroxidation damage rather than as repair agents [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R3].

## How anthocyanins exert antioxidant effects

Anthocyanins exert antioxidant effects through three interrelated mechanisms: **free radical elimination**, **enhancement of antioxidant enzyme activity**, and **reduction of lipid peroxidation damage**. Below is an integrated explanation, organized by each mechanism and supported by the evidence from the branch reports.

## 1. Free radical elimination: direct scavenging of reactive species

Anthocyanins primarily act as direct antioxidants by scavenging **free radicals** and **reactive oxygen and nitrogen species** (ROS and RNS). The evidence states that anthocyanins and anthocyanidins are good antioxidants because they scavenge free radicals and other reactive oxygen and nitrogen species [N1-F1]. This mechanism operates through two main biochemical pathways: **hydrogen atom transfer** (HAT) and **single-electron transfer** (SET) [N1-F1]. In HAT, a free radical removes a hydrogen atom from the antioxidant, converting the radical into a more stable product while forming a free radical of the antioxidant; in SET, the antioxidant donates an electron to the free radical, also forming a radical of the antioxidant [N1-F1]. The review also notes that the antioxidant activity of anthocyanins can be explained by their ability to donate electrons or hydrogen atoms from hydroxyl moieties to free radicals [N1-F1].

Structure-activity relationships are central to this mechanism. The evidence shows that methylation of the 4′-OH group markedly reduced antioxidant activity, indicating that hydroxyl substituents are important for radical scavenging [N1-R4]. This supports the idea that anthocyanin structure determines reactivity: hydroxyl groups, glycosylation, and acylation all influence stability and antioxidant capacity [N1-F1]. Glycosylation increases stability and water solubility, and increasing the number of sugar residues further increases stability by strengthening intramolecular hydrogen bonding and sugar-aglycone interactions [N1-F1].

The evidence also indicates that anthocyanins can directly neutralize reactive species through direct antioxidant properties and indirectly via induction of intracellular Nrf2 pathways [N1-R3]. This means that anthocyanins may stabilize radicals both by donating hydrogen or electrons and by activating downstream antioxidant defenses [N1-R2][N1-R3].

---

The evidence states that anthocyanins induce the activation of phase II antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes through the **Keap1/Nrf2/ARE pathway** [N2-R3]. When Nrf2 is activated, it translocates to the nucleus and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE), thereby inducing the transcription of phase II genes [N4-F2]. The review further notes that the activated Nrf2/ARE pathway boosts the expression of phase II genes either by Keap1-dependent or Keap1-independent means [N4-R1]. This provides a direct molecular explanation for how anthocyanins influence enzyme activity.

The phase II enzymes involved in this pathway include **glutathione S-transferase** (GST), **NAD(P)H: quinone oxidoreductase 1** (NQO1), and other phase II enzymes involved in detoxification and elimination of oxidative stress [N4-F2]. The evidence also highlights that phase II enzymes have long been studied for their preventative and protective effects against mutagens and carcinogens [N4-R3]. In addition, the anthocyanin study specifically points to activation of phase II antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes, indicating that anthocyanins are not only direct scavengers but also enzyme inducers [N2-R3].

Anthocyanins influence **transcription factors and signaling pathways** primarily through Nrf2-mediated regulation. By activating Nrf2, anthocyanins shift the balance toward phase II gene expression and away from the cytoplasmic sequestration of Nrf2 by Keap1 [N4-F2]. The evidence also notes that anthocyanin effects are context-dependent because the contribution of HAT and SET mechanisms depends on structure, solubility, partition coefficients, and solvent polarity [N1-F1]. This means that the enhancement of enzyme activity is not uniform but depends on the cellular and molecular environment [N1-F1].

Dose- and context-dependent effects are also evident. The evidence notes that anthocyanins can ameliorate human retinal capillary endothelial function by decreasing ROS and increasing the enzyme activity of catalase (CAT) [N2-R4]. This suggests that enzyme activation is tissue-specific and condition-dependent, rather than a universal effect [N2-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a dose- and context-dependent enhancement of antioxidant enzyme activity, with Nrf2-mediated induction of phase II enzymes as a central mechanism [N2-R3][N4-F2].

## 3. Reduction of lipid peroxidation damage

Anthocyanins reduce **lipid peroxidation damage** by lowering products such as **malondialdehyde (MDA)** and related markers of oxidative damage. These findings support the idea that anthocyanins reduce peroxidation damage by limiting the initiation and propagation of lipid peroxidation chains.

## 4. Overall antioxidant context and limitations

The overall antioxidant context of anthocyanins suggests that their strongest benefit is in **tissues and conditions where oxidative stress is elevated** and where anthocyanins can induce antioxidant defenses and reduce oxidative damage. ## How anthocyanins exert antioxidant effects

Anthocyanins exert antioxidant effects through three interrelated mechanisms: **free radical elimination**, **enhancement of antioxidant enzyme activity**, and **reduction of lipid peroxidation damage**. These mechanisms are not isolated; they overlap and depend on molecular structure, cellular context, and metabolic processing. Below is an integrated explanation, organized by each mechanism and supported by the evidence from the branch reports.

---

## 1. Free radical elimination: direct scavenging of reactive species

Anthocyanins primarily act as direct antioxidants by scavenging **free radicals** and **reactive oxygen and nitrogen species** (ROS and RNS). The evidence states that anthocyanins and anthocyanidins are good antioxidants because they scavenge free radicals and other reactive oxygen and nitrogen species [N1-F1]. This mechanism operates through two main biochemical pathways: **hydrogen atom transfer** (HAT) and **single-electron transfer** (SET) [N1-F1]. In HAT, a free radical removes a hydrogen atom from the antioxidant, converting the radical into a more stable product while forming a free radical of the antioxidant; in SET, the antioxidant donates an electron to the free radical, also forming a radical of the antioxidant [N1-F1]. The review also notes that the antioxidant activity of anthocyanins can be explained by their ability to donate electrons or hydrogen atoms from hydroxyl moieties to free radicals [N1-F1].

Structure-activity relationships are central to this mechanism. The evidence shows that methylation of the 4′-OH group markedly reduced antioxidant activity, indicating that hydroxyl substituents are important for radical scavenging [N1-R4]. This supports the idea that anthocyanin structure determines reactivity: hydroxyl groups, glycosylation, and acylation all influence stability and antioxidant capacity [N1-F1]. Glycosylation increases stability and water solubility, and increasing the number of sugar residues further increases stability by strengthening intramolecular hydrogen bonding and sugar-aglycone interactions [N1-F1].

The evidence also indicates that anthocyanins can directly neutralize reactive species through direct antioxidant properties and indirectly via induction of intracellular Nrf2 pathways [N1-R3]. This means that anthocyanins may stabilize radicals both by donating hydrogen or electrons and by activating downstream antioxidant defenses [N1-R2][N1-R3].

---

## 2. Enhancement of antioxidant enzyme activity

Anthocyanins also enhance antioxidant defense by **upregulating or activating antioxidant enzymes**. The evidence states that anthocyanins induce the activation of phase II antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes through the **Keap1/Nrf2/ARE pathway** [N2-R3]. Nrf2 is a master regulator of antioxidant defense, and the evidence explains that Nrf2 regulates the expression of a multitude of antioxidant and phase II enzyme genes, while Keap1 normally negatively regulates Nrf2 by sequestering it in the cytoplasm [N4-R4]. When Nrf2 is activated, it translocates to the nucleus and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE), thereby inducing the transcription of phase II genes [N4-F2]. The review further notes that the activated Nrf2/ARE pathway boosts the expression of phase II genes either by Keap1-dependent or Keap1-independent means [N4-R1]. This provides a direct molecular explanation for how anthocyanins influence enzyme activity.

The phase II enzymes involved in this pathway include **glutathione S-transferase** (GST), **NAD(P)H: quinone oxidoreductase 1** (NQO1), and other phase II enzymes involved in detoxification and elimination of oxidative stress [N4-F2]. The evidence also highlights that phase II enzymes have long been studied for their preventative and protective effects against mutagens and carcinogens [N4-R3]. In addition, the anthocyanin study specifically points to activation of phase II antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes, indicating that anthocyanins are not only direct scavengers but also enzyme inducers [N2-R3].

Anthocyanins influence **transcription factors and signaling pathways** primarily through Nrf2-mediated regulation. By activating Nrf2, anthocyanins shift the balance toward phase II gene expression and away from the cytoplasmic sequestration of Nrf2 by Keap1 [N4-F2]. The evidence also notes that anthocyanin effects are context-dependent because the contribution of HAT and SET mechanisms depends on structure, solubility, partition coefficients, and solvent polarity [N1-F1]. This means that the enhancement of enzyme activity is not uniform but depends on the cellular and molecular environment [N1-F1].

Dose- and context-dependent effects are also evident. The evidence notes that anthocyanins can ameliorate human retinal capillary endothelial function by decreasing ROS and increasing the enzyme activity of catalase (CAT) [N2-R4]. This suggests that enzyme activation is tissue-specific and condition-dependent, rather than a universal effect [N2-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a dose- and context-dependent enhancement of antioxidant enzyme activity, with Nrf2-mediated induction of phase II enzymes as a central mechanism [N2-R3][N4-F2].

---

## 3. Reduction of lipid peroxidation damage

Anthocyanins reduce **lipid peroxidation damage** by lowering products such as **malondialdehyde (MDA)** and related markers of oxidative damage. This implies that anthocyanins may improve membrane integrity by reducing the formation of peroxidation products that compromise membrane structure and function.

The overall antioxidant context of anthocyanins suggests that their strongest benefit is in **tissues and conditions where oxidative stress is elevated** and where anthocyanins can induce antioxidant defenses and reduce oxidative damage. The review on anthocyanin antioxidant activity states that the best evidence is from cell-free systems, in vitro, animal experiments, and human studies, but also notes uncertainties associated with these studies [N1-F1]. The human study cited in the evidence shows that dietary anthocyanins can improve antioxidant defenses, while the animal studies provide more direct evidence of lipid peroxidation reduction and DNA damage reduction [N3-F3][N5-R4]. Anthocyanins are absorbed, transported, and metabolized primarily as **metabolites after gut microbiota processing**. The review also notes that microbiota catabolism produces new metabolites that may be absorbed and induce biological effects, suggesting that the bioavailable pool consists largely of these metabolites [N6-R4].

Gut microbiota and metabolic processing affect antioxidant activity by altering the **forms of anthocyanins available to exert effects**. The evidence states that anthocyanins are metabolized by gut microbiota into metabolites, which may then be absorbed and exert biological effects [N6-R4]. This means that the antioxidant activity observed in vivo is not necessarily due to the intact anthocyanin molecule but to its metabolites. The review on anthocyanin bioavailability further notes that microbiota catabolism can alter anthocyanin structure and activity, which is relevant because antioxidant effects depend on molecular form [N6-R4]. ---

## Integrated conclusion

Anthocyanins exert antioxidant effects through a combination of **direct free radical elimination**, **enhancement of antioxidant enzyme activity**, and **reduction of lipid peroxidation damage**. They act primarily by scavenging free radicals and reactive oxygen and nitrogen species via HAT and SET, and by activating Nrf2-regulated phase II enzymes that boost detoxification and antioxidant defenses [N1-F1][N2-R3][N4-F2]. They also reduce lipid peroxidation products such as MDA and oxidative damage markers, with evidence suggesting a preventive rather than reparative role in peroxidation damage [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R3].
